name: Aaron Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lineman for the power company in my hometown, up in the hills. My grandfather strung some of the lines I fix, and my dad did thirty-four years on the same crew. Most days I'm on the trouble truck, which means I go wherever the power's out: a squirrel in a transformer, a tree on the line up Chapel Hill Road, an old fuse. I know half the people whose lights I put back on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is being useful in your own town. An old lady brings you a coffee in a flask after a storm, that's worth something. What wears me down is the paperwork and the new apps the company keeps pushing, I'd rather just do the job. I'm engaged to Lucia, wedding's next autumn, and we're building a house on a piece of land my dad gave us. Between that and the savings, we're in good shape, thank God.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, it's a fad. At church people talk about it like it's the end of the world, and I'd tell them it's just another gadget. I don't post online, Lucia does all that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me. Wires still break, trees still fall, people still need a man to come fix it. That's been true for three generations in my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, finish the house, get married. Nothing changes. Maybe I'd do more overtime this winter to pay for the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, honestly. That's the world I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. The company put some assistant thing on the work tablets and I've never opened it. If I need to know something, I ring my dad or ask the old foreman, Walt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, course it's hype, robots can't climb a pole in the snow. He's been saying that since I was a kid. In this picture he'd be right.

S0.say: He'd say he told everyone it was a fad, and he'd tell worried people at church it's just another gadget. He leaves posting online to his fiancée.
S0.think: He thinks it means nothing for him, since wires still break, trees still fall and people still need someone to fix them, as has been true for three generations of his family.
S0.do: Keeps working, finishes building the house and gets married as planned. Might take more overtime this winter to pay for the kitchen.
S0.feel: Calm and glad, because this is the world he wants.
S0.quote: Wires still break, trees still fall, people still need a man to come fix it.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron's identity is bound up with his family's three generations on the same lines and his place in the town. He has never opened the AI assistant on his work tablet and prefers to ask his father or an old foreman. Faith and community come through in his language.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly city jobs that'll change, office work. Up here we'll keep doing what we do. I'd tell the younger guys not to worry too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a little sore about it. Every new thing the company brings in means more time on screens and less time on poles. But my job would still be there, I'm fairly sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd learn whatever they make me learn and not a minute more. Get married, move into the house, keep my head down and wait to see what actually changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit grumpy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company starts pushing AI on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it if I had to, like the tablet. I'd grumble, I'd ask Walt to show me, and I'd do it wrong for a month. Then I'd get used to it, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think gains from this kind of change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people selling it, mainly, and the company bosses. That's fine, that's business. It's when they start telling you how to live your life with it that I'd have a problem.

S1.say: He'd say mostly city office jobs will change, while work in the hills carries on. He'd tell younger colleagues not to worry too much.
S1.think: Privately he'd be a little sore that every new thing means more screen time and less pole time. Still, he's fairly sure his job would remain.
S1.do: Learns only what the company requires, gets married and moves into the new house. Keeps his head down and waits to see what actually changes.
S1.quote: Every new thing the company brings in means more time on screens and less time on poles.
S1.fieldNote: His complaint is about screens replacing pole time, not about losing his job. He accepts businesses profiting from technology as normal and draws his line at being told how to live. He would adapt slowly and grudgingly, leaning on an older colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say I don't believe it, not in two years, not up here. But I'd also say families and churches are going to have to look after each other, because I don't trust anyone in a city to do it for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if a robot can do my job in two years, then it's not just me, it's my dad's whole life's work gone. I've never done anything else. I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the house where it is, roof on and walls up, and finish the inside ourselves slowly instead of paying builders. I'd save every bit of overtime. And I'd sit down with my dad and my uncles and work out how we'd all get by, because that's what families do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I wouldn't say it out loud, but I'd be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The wedding is next autumn. Does this change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd make it smaller. Family, church, a meal in the hall instead of a big place. Lucia would be upset for about a week and then she'd say it was the right call. We'd still get married, though, that wouldn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't like handouts. What if there's no work at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's hard. I'd still want to work, even if it's fixing fences for the neighbours. But if there's nothing, there's nothing. I'd lean on family first and the church second, and I'd hate taking anything from the government, but I wouldn't let Lucia go hungry over pride.

S2.say: He'd say he doesn't believe it, not in two years and not in the hills. He'd add that families and churches will have to look after each other because he doesn't trust city people to do it.
S2.think: He thinks that if a robot can do his job in two years, his father's life's work goes with it. He has never done anything else and wouldn't know where to start.
S2.do: Stops the house build once the roof and walls are up, finishing the inside himself, and saves every bit of overtime. Makes the wedding smaller and plans with his father and uncles how the family would get by.
S2.feel: Scared, though he wouldn't say so out loud.
S2.quote: I'd hate taking anything from the government, but I wouldn't let Lucia go hungry over pride.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits his family identity hardest; he spoke of his father's work being erased. When I raised the contradiction about handouts, he set an order: family, then church, then government as a last resort. The wedding shrinks but goes ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, I'll believe it when I see it. Maybe I'd add that people should get their houses in order, pay off debts, look after their own. That's how my family's always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years still feels fast for someone like me. I'm not a learner of new things. I'd be thirty-two and starting over, and I don't know what at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the house properly, but without a loan, so we own it outright when it lands. My dad's got a woodlot, and I'd start selling firewood on weekends with him, a bit of extra money that a robot isn't going to bother with soon. And we'd go ahead with the wedding as planned, maybe hold off a bit on kids until we see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not sleepless, but worried most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the years before it lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekends for the woodlot, weekdays on the truck, every spare coin into the house. No debt by the time it comes. That's the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything your dad's generation did that you'd copy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the mill closed, my grandfather's brothers all helped each other build houses and found work for each other. Nobody waited for anyone. I'd want to be like that.

S3.say: He'd repeat that he'll believe it when he sees it, and advise people to get their houses in order, pay off debts and look after their own, as his family always has.
S3.think: He thinks five years is still fast for someone who doesn't learn new things easily. At thirty-two he'd be starting over without knowing what at.
S3.do: Finishes the house without a loan so they own it outright, and starts selling firewood from his father's woodlot on weekends. Goes ahead with the wedding but holds off on children until things are clearer.
S3.feel: Worried most days, though not sleepless.
S3.quote: Weekends for the woodlot, weekdays on the truck, every spare coin into the house.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, he chooses debt-free ownership and a family side business rather than retraining. He drew on a family story about a mill closure where relatives helped each other. Holding off on children came up quietly and seemed to matter to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a lot can happen in ten years, and nobody knows. I'd tell people to work hard, stay close to family and not panic. That's what I'd say at church too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years worries me in a different way. That's right when we'd have little ones. I'd be thirty-seven with two kids under five, and that's the worst time to lose your work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with work, keep the firewood going with my dad and grow it a bit, and keep paying the house down. I wouldn't learn a new trade, I'll be honest. I'd just make sure we're as solid as we can be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, oddly more than with five. It's further off, but it lands on the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me and hurts me. It helps because I've got time to pay things off. It hurts because by then I've got more people depending on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids, if you have them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them their dad and their grandad and their great-grandad kept the lights on in this town. And that whatever they end up doing, they do it properly, robots or not.

S4.say: He'd say a lot can happen in ten years, nobody knows, and people should work hard, stay close to family and not panic. He'd say the same at church.
S4.think: He thinks ten years worries him differently, because it lands just when he expects to have small children. At thirty-seven with two children under five would be the worst time to lose work.
S4.do: Carries on working, grows the firewood business with his father and keeps paying down the house. Admits he wouldn't learn a new trade but would make the family as financially solid as possible.
S4.feel: Anxious, oddly more so than with five years, because the timing falls on his future children.
S4.quote: It's further off, but it lands on the kids.
S4.fieldNote: This was the surprise of the interview: a longer warning made him slightly more worried, because the arrival date lines up with having young children. He rules out retraining and relies on property, family business and family. His pride in his family's place in the town stayed strong to the end.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because we'd have the house half-built and the wedding coming. But the ten-year one bothers me more than I thought it would, because of kids. What would help is the company keeping local men on as long as it can, and people in town sticking together like they used to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the towns. When a factory closes, people notice. When the power company quietly stops needing linemen, nobody will notice until the old lady with the coffee has a robot at her door instead of me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I needed.

headlineQuote: When the power company quietly stops needing linemen, nobody will notice until the old lady with the coffee has a robot at her door instead of me.
portrait: Aaron Alvarez is a 27-year-old third-generation lineman on the trouble truck in his hill-country hometown, where he knows many of the people whose power he restores. Engaged to Lucia, with a wedding next autumn and a house going up on land his father gave him, he has never opened the AI assistant on his work tablet. He is calm through the milder pictures, grumbling only about screens. Fast AGI alarms him as a threat to his family's life's work; he would shrink the wedding, pause the house and lean on family and church before the government. With more time he plans a debt-free house and a firewood business with his father, and a ten-year warning worries him because it would land when his children are small.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, with the house half-built and the wedding coming, though the ten-year picture bothers him because it would arrive when he has small children.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping local workers on as long as possible, and people in town sticking together as they used to.
